evidence_establishes: Opponent next-possession PPP after specific play types contains a small but real suppression component for some play types (CUT, TRANSITION, SPOT_UP, POST_UP) when estimated with matched controls and placebo checks (SF-APPS-075).
The magnitude of opponent-next suppression is approximately 0.01-0.02 PPP, which is small relative to direct PPP differences between play types.
DRIVE does not show a real opponent-next suppression effect (SF-APPS-075).
Play-type net swing (own PPP minus opponent next PPP) alters rankings compared with own PPP alone, most notably making DRIVE and POST_UP appear worse (SF-APPM-011, SF-APPS-049).

Own-sequence PPP lag effects (action memory) are artefactual when global comparisons are used and disappear after within-team demeaning; there is essentially no within-team possession-to-possession memory from one own play type to the next own PPP (SF-APPS-073, SF-CHT-029).
Season-to-season stability of sequential suppressors for individual stars is very low (SF-APPA-058).
evidence_does_not_establish: Whether the observed opponent-next suppression magnitudes are 'large enough' to justify AVOID play-type labels against any practical or decision-theoretic threshold.
The stability and generalisability of opponent-next suppression across different team contexts, lineups, and seasons at the play-type level.
Whether own-sequence lags could exist at a finer granularity (e.g., player-level, within specific tactical contexts) that was not detected by the within-team aggregate approach.
A validated, reproducible pipeline for converting opponent-next PPP estimates into reliable AVOID labels without overfitting.
own_inferences: The opponent-next PPP component of play types, while statistically detectable for some play types, is probably too small (≈0.01–0.02 PPP) to drive a meaningful AVOID label in a typical NBA decision-making context, where effect sizes below 0.05 PPP are unlikely to change play-calling strategy.
Attempting to build AVOID labels solely from opponent-next PPP without a pre-specified, practically grounded threshold would risk over-interpreting noise and producing unstable recommendations.
Own-sequence lags as a candidate for driving labels are fundamentally unsupported by the data; any apparent effect is confounded by between-team differences and vanishes under a within-team design.
uncertainties: The research question does not define 'large enough'; the threshold for an AVOID label is implicit and may refer to practical significance, statistical significance, or a decision-rule not stated.

The existing evidence on opponent-next PPP uses earlier seasons; the three additional seasons of data (2022-23 to 2025-26) could yield more precise estimates and reveal heterogeneity, but are unlikely to change the effect-size order of magnitude.

The question originally mentions 'own-sequence lags similarly matter'; the historical evidence strongly contradicts that claim, but it is unclear whether the proposer is aware of the artefact findings.

historical_effect.explanation: Without the historical retrieval, one might launch a broad exploration of opponent next-PPP and own-sequence lags to discover AVOID labels. The retrieval shows that own-sequence lags are an established artifact (within-team), and opponent-next suppression is real but very small. This shifts the decision from a greenfield exploration to a sceptical, pre-registered quantification of opponent-next effects against a pre-specified practical threshold, with own-sequence testing explicitly deprioritised unless the within-team artefact is addressed.

blocking_constraints.text: Opponent next-PPP is influenced by game state, opponent defensive strength, and lineup quality. Without rigorous matching or adjustment, estimated play-type effects will be biased.
Testing many play types, possibly across multiple lags and team contexts, inflates the false-positive rate unless appropriate corrections (e.g., Bonferroni, Benjamini-Hochberg) are planned.
If AVOID labels are derived from the same data used to test the question, the analysis becomes circular unless labels are defined on held-out data or a pre-registered rule.
Rare play types such as PUTBACK have far fewer possessions, producing wide confidence intervals that may prevent reliable AVOID classification.

The true effect sizes are so small relative to possession-level PPP variance that distinguishing a genuine 0.02 PPP suppression from zero requires very large samples, and achieving practical significance (e.g., 0.05 PPP) is unlikely.

prior_work.summary: Opponent-next PPP after play types has been estimated and found to be statistically real for some play types but the effects are very small. Own-sequence PPP lags are artefactual. Play-type net swing re-ranks play types but the magnitude of opponent-next components is unlikely to drive AVOID labels without a very low practical threshold.

risks.text: Game-state (score margin, period), opponent defensive quality, and lineup strength confound opponent next-PPP; improper control could produce spurious play-type effects.
Rare play types (PUTBACK, POST_UP in some contexts) have limited samples, making it difficult to estimate opponent-next PPP with enough precision to classify AVOID.
If all play types are tested for AVOID labels simultaneously without correction, some may be labelled incorrectly by chance.
Defining AVOID labels directly from the observed opponent-next PPP in the same dataset without an independent holdout risks overfitting and label instability.
The effect sizes are so small (≈0.01-0.02 PPP) that even if statistically significant, they fall below likely practical significance thresholds for changing play-calling strategy.
The reliability of the underlying play-type labels (from the graph database built on NBA play-by-play) could introduce noise, especially for ambiguous actions.
Play-type effectiveness and opponent responses may drift over seasons due to rule changes, strategic trends, and personnel shifts, so effects estimated on older seasons may not hold in 2025-26.

design.estimand: Average difference in opponent next-possession PPP (points scored by the opponent on the possession immediately following a labeled play-type initiation) between play type X and a matched baseline of other play-type possessions, after accounting for game state and team quality.
design.unit: Opponent possession immediately following a labeled play-type possession by the focal team.
design.sample: All plays from NBA 2022-23 through 2025-26 (regular season and playoffs) with a valid next possession within the same period, excluding garbage time (margin >20 at start of possession in 4th quarter), end-of-quarter possessions with no immediate next play, and possessions where the next opponent possession starts with free throws on a continuation.
design.power: For common play types (n > 100,000), the minimum detectable effect size at 80% power and α = 0.005 (Bonferroni for 10 tests) is approximately 0.007 PPP. For rare types like PUTBACK (n ≈ 20,000), MDE ≈ 0.016 PPP. Power for a practical threshold of 0.05 PPP is >0.99 for common types and >0.80 for most rare types.
design.controls: Exact matching or regression adjustment for: score margin (binned into trailing large/small, tied, leading small/large), period, opponent season defensive rating, home/away, proxy for lineup strength (e.g., number of starters on floor for each team), and whether the preceding possession ended in a dead ball. For own-sequence lags (if tested), mandatory within-team-season demeaning as used in SF-APPS-073.
design.falsification: Placebo test: re-assign opponent next-PPP to a randomly selected possession from the same game and period, not the one immediately following the focal play type; expect null effect. Additionally, test that opponent next-PPP after a timeout or quarter break shows no systematic difference. For own-sequence lags, confirm that lag-2 effect is zero after within-team adjustment.
design.multiplicity: Bonferroni correction across the set of tested play types (8-10). Own-sequence lags, if separately tested, form an independent family with its own correction. Pre-register the list of play types and thresholds.
design.decision_rule: A play type is labelled AVOID if the lower bound of the one-sided 95% confidence interval for its opponent-next PPP effect (using a harmful direction: opponent PPP above baseline) exceeds 0.05 PPP (practically meaningful detriment). Conversely, a PREFER label could be assigned if the upper bound of opponent-next PPP is below -0.05 PPP (suppression). The thresholds should be justified with domain input.
